query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive model that explicitly incorporates chemical short‐range order (SRO) and the ensuing local lattice distortions will decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr, yielding lattice thermal conductivity predictions with at least a 20% higher accuracy compared to traditional Debye-based approaches developed for ideal, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy fabricated under controlled conditions (minimal oxygen and extrinsic defects) with a primarily random solid solution that nonetheless embeds measurable SRO and local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Development and application of a computational framework that integrates atomistic simulations (including SRO characterization) and refined phonon scattering calculations, separating lattice contribution from electronic conductivity.
generation.conditions: Applicability is restricted to oxygen-controlled (≤1 wt.%) and nearly defect-free samples over a temperature range from 300 K to 1200 K, with additional comparisons in the low-temperature regime (<200 K) where lattice and electronic contributions are experimentally observed to be comparable.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range order and the concomitant local lattice distortions, which modify phonon scattering rates.
generation.mechanism: By capturing the atomic-scale effects of SRO on local lattice distortions, the model more accurately simulates phonon scattering independent of electron transport. This approach addresses the oversimplification of a uniform Debye temperature and thereby prevents conflation of lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity values that deviate by less than ±10% from experimental measurements in the high-temperature range (300–1200 K) and will reveal a clear separation between phononic and electronic transport regimes in low-temperature (below 200 K) measurements.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical approaches based on Debye-temperature approximations and DFT-derived elastic properties for perfect, defect-free crystals.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only to samples where oxygen content is minimal and extrinsic defects are controlled; it may not hold in materials with significant oxidation or structural imperfections that introduce additional scattering mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how dominant the impact of SRO and local lattice distortions is in the separation of lattice and electronic contributions, especially at low temperatures where both mechanisms interplay; further empirical validation is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with controlled, low oxygen levels (<1 wt.%) and minimal defects, and another with standard oxygen content. Measure the temperature-dependent total thermal conductivity using techniques capable of decoupling phonon and electron contributions (e.g., time-domain thermoreflectance combined with electrical conductivity measurements) over the ranges below 200 K and between 300–1200 K.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity extracted in the 300–1200 K range
Separation of lattice and electronic contributions in the <200 K regime
Comparison of measured phonon scattering rates versus model predictions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive model does not yield lattice thermal conductivity values with at least a 20% improvement over the accuracy of Debye-based methods, or if the expected decoupling of transport channels at low temperatures is not experimentally observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
SignificanceMetallic alloys underpin many technological advancements. In these materials two or more chemical elements are mixed together, often forming phases in which elements are spread out in an almost random manner. The tendency of certain chemical motifs to be more common than others—known as chemical short-range order—renders alloys “slightly less random than completely random.” Short-range order affects the stability and properties of metals, besides being the harbinger of important phenomena such as phase transitions. ## Abstract
AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.
